content: Lactuca virosa, commonly known as Wild Lettuce, Bitter Lettuce, Opium Lettuce, Poisonous Lettuce, or Rakutu-Karyumu-So, is a legal ethnobotanical substance in the United States. It is botanically related to common lettuce (Lactuca sativa). In the 19th century, Lactuca virosa was utilized by physicians as a substitute when opium was unavailable. In 1911, the Council of the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain conducted extensive studies on the plant and identified two key chemical compounds responsible for its effects: lactucopicrin and lactucin. During the 1970s, the plant experienced a resurgence in popularity in the United States. Currently, it is classified as unscheduled by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), meaning it is legal to grow, purchase, and possess without the need for a prescription or license. The effects of consuming Lactuca virosa are reported to be similar to those of opium, although the plant does not contain any opiates. The effects are typically felt quickly but are short-lived, lasting from approximately 30 minutes to a few hours, and gradually taper off. Historically, the plant has been used as an anesthetic, a sleep aid, and recreationally. Oils and extracts derived from Lactuca virosa are often incorporated into teas to promote sleep. The greens of the plant are sometimes added to salads, although the leaves are notably more bitter than other salad greens. The plant can also be smoked, either in the form of dried leaves or a sticky resinous extract obtained from the leaves. Additionally, beverages can be prepared by soaking the leaves in alcohol. Lactuca virosa contains flavonoids, which exhibit potent antioxidant properties. It also contains coumarins and N-methyl-β-phenethylamine. Furthermore, the plant has been identified as a galactagogue, a substance that enhances breast milk production, particularly when used in combination with alfalfa.
